object_transcript:
Artist Bio:
Adrienne Domnick is a multidisciplinary artist from Mississippi whose work is an exploration of celebrating black culture. She is best known for her large-scale hard-edge portraits. Her creative path weaves narratives that honor the resilience and creativity of black heroes, aiming to inspire and deepen society’s understanding of their impact.

Social / Website:
Website: www.adriennedomnick.art 

 Instagram: adriennedomnick

Exhibition Text:
Since 2011, Adrienne Domnick has developed her artistic craft through a variety of mediums. As a multidisciplinary artist, Domnick creates work that responds to the social environment she grew up and lives in today. Inspired by the idea of the less focused “b-side” of records, this exhibition explores an ongoing journey and creative project that Domnick has worked on since the beginning of her artistic career. B SIDES serves as a cultural archive and music catalog delivered through a dynamic and bold series of paintings. This exhibition visually delivers a story of growth; growth of the artist and of the cultural impact of the musical artists featured. Domnick’s large scale paintings elevate her subjects to a larger than life status, lifting up the subject and memorializing these artists’ legacy and influence on the world around them. As a self described archivist, Domnick draws from an extensive record of music, books, and fashion when creating her art; striving to document and preserve Black culture in all of her work.

title: Self Censorship
creator: Emma Lorenz
description:
"This work contains several aspects of my practice, including the use of printmaking, repurposed thrifted objects, and the use of self portraiture to comment on expectations about personal expression and body." 

The woodblock prints in Self Censorship were made using model poses and photographs from Vogue Magazine as the source material. Three images were selected, and then by superimposing my own plus size body onto the models, I created new drawings, which were then carved into the MDF woodblock prints. 

Traditionally, these models are considered the height of beauty and desirability by society, and by appropriating the forms their bodies take with my own non conventional body, I am making myself the object of desire. 

The prints and forms are obscured and “censored” however, by the use of screenprinting inks. In this, I am grappling with my own feelings of shame and discomfort, in expressing that sexuality or desirability to a wider audience.

object_transcript:
Artist Bio:
Emma Lorenz describes herself as a found object/mixed media artist, utilizing processes such as printmaking, bookmaking, papermaking and object fabrication to create artwork that discusses body image and identity. Originally from Dallas Texas, Lorenz is currently living and making art in Jackson Mississippi. She teaches studio classes on the weekend at the Mississippi Museum of Art and works full time at the Mississippi Museum of Natural Science. Her work has been featured in local exhibitions such as The Mash-Up: Home is Where the Art is, at the Arts Center of Mississippi, as well as work in the permanent collection of the Ohio University Printmaking Archives, the Fat Print Archives and . She graduated from Millsaps College in 2024, with a Bachelor's Degree in Studio Art, and a Minor in Psychology.

Social / Website:
Instagram: @a_stitch_to_press
Website: emmalorenz.weebly.com

Exhibition Text:
In this exhibition, A Retrospective of Self, Emma Lorenz offers a voice to often underrepresented and judged groups and vulnerably invites the viewer into her internal discourse and process of self discovery. The physical nature of Lorenz’s work and the use of materials such as embroidery, cyanotypes, and papercraft provides a more tangible connection to the viewer. Secondhand objects are important to Lorenz’s practice as they bring into question the lives of these objects and furniture before they are found by her. In her work Lorenz employs three methods of creating: repurposing, mimicry and fabrication, and deconstruction. The contrast between the familiarity of everyday objects and the exploration of traditionally “taboo” subjects such as weight, gender, and sexuality allow Lorenz to deconstruct societal expectations and challenge the viewer’s preconceived notions of these issues. This idea of the home and personal identity begins with the open suitcase, bringing to mind the idea of “unpacking” both the physical work in this exhibition as well as the artist’s internal thoughts and creative practice.

title: FVLLING
creator: Fooly
description:
VLLING examines the themes of chaos and control, disorientation, and the human instinct to grasp for stability. The subject is captured in mid-fall, surrounded by a swirling vortex of sharp, jagged patterns that evoke a sense of spiraling descent. The grayscale subject, dressed in casual contemporary attire, reaches out against the oppressive black and white maelstrom, providing a stark contrast to the tumultuous backdrop.

The feeling of movement is palpable, drawing the viewer into the unsettling experience of losing one's footing. The artwork is a masterful depiction of the sudden shifts that can occur in life's trajectory, the unpredictable moments that upend balance and certainty. Goliday's use of perspective and the illusion of depth creates a realistic sensation of falling, inviting empathy and reflection on the viewer's own experiences with upheaval and the fight for composure amidst life's challenges.

Artist Bio:
Victoria Meek was raised in Meridian, Mississippi and has been based in Jackson since 2017. She received a B.F.A. in Painting & Drawing from the University of Southern Mississippi. And an M.A. in Museum Studies from New York University. Victoria has been in group exhibitions at Peter Freeman, Inc, New York; Pearl River Glass Studio; and Millsaps College. “Trees” is her first solo show. This Municipal Art Gallery exhibition focuses on drawings & paintings of trees or things in relationship with them. Much of the work was made between 2023-24, a period Victoria dedicated to observing and imagining trees in Jackson.

Social / Website:
instagram: v.r.meek

Exhibition Text:
Trees is a focused exploration of the natural environment of central Mississippi through the eyes of Victoria Meek. Finding peace and restoration in nature is key to Meek’s practice; working in Jackson, Mississippi, Meek observes her surrounding environment with a keen interest in the accessibility of trees and their reliable presence as subjects for her work. When selecting a model Meek considers details such as the sway and movement of the tree, seeing them as dancers with their own sense of identity and drama. In addition to the natural world Meek is inspired by tradition defying artists such as Edouard Manet and Pierre Bonnard and like them Meek works en plein air observing her environment. Meek also finds inspiration in contemporary artists such as Jennifer Packer whose intentional incompleteness in her work aligns with Meek’s priority of creative process over the finished product in her artistic practice. In this exhibition Meek presents a collection of recent oil paintings, watercolors, and pencil drawings which despite the traditional medium explore her natural surroundings through a uniquely personal viewpoint.

title: Channel 3 (graphics on tv)
creator: Brenden Davis
description:
This piece was created during my time working as a graphic artist at WLBT 3 News, one of central Mississippi's most iconic media institutions. Channel 3 (graphics on tv) captures a moment of lived experience shaped by the unique intersections of creative labor, media production, and Southern identity. It also contributes to the preservation of local narratives and honors the creative workers behind the scenes of Mississippi’s creative media landscape.

Created during my time as a graphic artist for WLBT 3 News, Channel 3 (graphics on tv) is a layered meditation on media labor, digital overload, and representation. A hunched figure stretches toward a laptop, surrounded by fragments of broadcast graphics, color marks, and overlapping forms. Elements of television production, such as the “title safe” overlay used to frame on-screen content, are repurposed as visual motifs that underscore the tension between clarity and constraint. The piece reflects on the often-invisible labor behind what becomes visible.

Artist Bio:
Brenden Davis (b. 1997) is a multidisciplinary artist based in Jackson, Mississippi, working across painting, graphic design, and animation. Davis explores surrealism, abstraction, and interpersonal experience, focusing on self-perception and social dynamics. Drawing from personal history and cultural influences, they create abstract figures and dreamlike landscapes that challenge societal narratives and invite viewers into alternate realities. Through their work, Davis seeks to captivate, provoke reflection, and foster meaningful dialogue.

Social / Website:
brendendavis.com

Exhibition Text:
Memory Corrupted: An Exploration of Time and Perception offers a carefully curated time capsule representing snapshots of artist Brenden Davis’ life experiences. Inspired by the way memories blur and reshape as time moves forward, Davis challenges expectation and creates complex visual narratives that breathe new life into traditional surrealist motifs. In these works Davis studies time and how his perception of the world around him has changed over the past eight years of his life. As an artist working with many mediums–including paint, clay, paper, and digital media–Davis is able to literally cut up and rearrange these visual representations of his memories and experiences to create a new, distorted interpretation of his journey through life. The vivid colors, chaotic style, and surreal nature of Davis’ work creates an opportunity for the viewer to find personal connections within the imagery despite the deeply personal nature of this archive.

title: Pretty Eyes
creator: Bro. Shambé Jones
description:
As an artist, Shambé creates art because he sees art as life. He feel that everything has a
design and purpose. He also creates art based on history that he has studied, nature, and
some of the materials that are used. His aim is to tap into the viewers subconscious and bring
forth healing visually.
He work in a variety of mediums but mostly in pyrography which is the burning of an image
onto a surface ( mostly wood and sometimes leather) with a hot metal tip. Many times he has
ideas that he wants to do , but he also lets the markings in the wood guide him in what image
he’s going to create. For Shambé , every mark is intentional. Wood selection is also important to
him. To help the environment he often use recycled materials donated from other artists and
craftspeople. With this medium one of his biggest challenges is adding color to the wood without
taking away from the sight of the wood grain itself. He doesn't want it to look like it has been
painted. He overcame this problem by using wood stains.
While using wood stain another problem occurred. He had to figure out a way to keep the
stain from running and going into places where it’s not wanted. Painters tape works but he has
trained himself to have more control of the stain along with a steady hand

Artist Bio:
Shambé Jones was born in the Midwest region. Champaign-Urbana Illinois where he started his creative journey at the age of 5. He grew up in a family full of artists, musicians, seamstresses, carpenters, photographers, farmers etc. There were also family friends who influenced his growth as an artist. He has always been inspired by music and nature and uses both of these muses to guide his process of creating. Visual art was the way in which he expressed not only how he interpreted the world, but it allowed him to vision the world the way he wanted to see it. 

By the time he reached high school, he began entering illustration contests and the arts is how he spent much of his time. Working to perfect his skills and find which platform would be his focus, he attended Jackson State University, where he earned a B.A. in Fine Arts. 

During his matriculation, he participated in the Jackson State University study abroad program in Côte D’Ivorie, Africa, where he spent the summer studying various forms of craftwork like sculpting, ceramics, brass casting, batik dying among other crafts. By way of Drew University this experience tremendously influenced his creativity and kinship to pyrography. He taught himself this art form in the year 2000 after being drawn to the handcraft skills he learned from the people of Coté D’Ivorie and natural elements (wood) that could be turned into art while being easily accessible. While pyrography is the visual art form that he is most drawn to, he continues to further his skills in painting, sculpture, ceramics, and mixed media. 
 
His process of creating work depends on what medium he’s using. It usually starts with ideas that are formed in his mind. Once there is a blueprint of what's to be done, additional study, planning and or research is next to guide and influence the work. The next step is to gather all material that is needed to create the piece visualized. After gathering the materials his next process is to prepare the surface to be burned, painted, drawn on or created with. This could be anything from sanding, priming, or putting a basic sketch on a canvas or paper. During this process he gets his atmosphere together so that he has a good positive environment to work in, which usually involves nice music and incense.

Artist Bio:
Art has been a part of George Miles Jr.’s life since he was in third grade. The artist, who creates art as Sky Miles, works in mediums such as photography, ceramics, watercolors, mixed media and more.

“I got into (art) because of my community and my parents,” Miles says. “It was an artist who came in and did a workshop and gave us guidelines, and the teacher was amazed at the project I did based on the tips, so I got the spark early on.”

Miles, a Starkville, Miss., native, received his associate’s degree in photojournalism from Hinds Community College in 2000, and went on to attend Jackson State University, where he graduated with a bachelor’s degree in liberal arts in 2002.“I formed a group of artists (that included ones such as Tony Davenport and Josh Hailey), and we started doing shows around the city. That’s when things started to take off; it became like a movement,” he says.Miles has worked for Ask For More Arts, which is a program of Ask For More Jackson (formerly known as Parents for Public Schools of Jackson) for the past seven years and has been its art director for three. The group’s goal is to build a creative foundation for students by incorporating art into the classrooms. He works with all students, from elementary to high school

title: Memory's Garden
creator: Greta Koshenina
description:
This artwork was one of the first pieces I created in the series that became "Warping Southern Myths," which I exhibited at the Arts Center. The digital collage combines photos of me as a child with a contemporary photograph of my friend Macon's backyard, located across the street from my parents' house, where I grew up, in Water Valley. As I ran across the street to hang out with him and my boyfriend, I reflected on the symbolism of remaining in the same place through different stages of life and the importance of play and joy. The top print includes photograms of flowers from my mom's garden and Macon's yard.

I'm deeply inspired by place, and when I created this piece, I was meditating on the meaning of home and how it shifts over time. I have called many places home over the years, but Water Valley's streets and woods hold childhood memories that are at once vivid and surreal like mythological tales. I look at the images of myself from years past, and I feel a tenderness for my younger self. This piece was inspired by a dream I had years ago, where I met my 5-year-old self in a field of wildflowers. This was a healing and transformative experience and dream, and since then, I have felt that version of Little Greta at peace.

Artist Bio:
Greta Koshenina is a multidisciplinary artist, documentarian, and curator from Water Valley, Mississippi. Koshenina earned a BA in Classics, an MA in Southern Studies, and an MFA in Documentary Expression from the University of Mississippi. Now based in Cleveland, MS, Koshenina is an adjunct professor at Delta State University. Along with Ben Powell and Graham Hamaker, Greta runs ALLUVIAL, a production company dedicated to telling Mississippi stories. Koshenina has received a Mississippi Arts Commission (MAC) Individual Project Grant, a MAC Mini-Grant, and Southern Studies' Sue Hart Award and Lucille and Motee Daniels Award. In July 2025, she showed her work in a solo exhibition at the Arts Center of Mississippi in Jackson, MS. Koshenina’s recent group exhibitions include ‘Heirloom’ at Dogwater Gallery, New Orleans, LA; ‘One Night Stand Motel Art Show,’ Oxford, MS; and ‘Miniatures’ at Bozarts Gallery, Water Valley, MS.

Social / Website:
www.gretakoshenina.com

insta: gretakoshenina

Exhibition Text:
Details fade upon waking from a dream; the mind forgets years of existence. As a multimedia installation artist, my work holds a moment and strips away the details, reminding us that what may seem concrete and captured is liminal and ephemeral. I combine cyanotype, film, and poetry in my installations, creating an immersive experience that guides the audience through a meditation on the soft underbelly of family mythology.

I stitch together cyanotypes printed on antique linens and archival paper to form cyanotype collages. My clumsy red stitches stand out, symbolizing the loss of a traditional, generational craft in my family.

My work explores the connection between spirit and the subconscious, as well as the personal and the universal. My art represents a journey to understand religion and spirituality from my perspective rather than a rigid viewpoint. I remain in Mississippi and retrace my past. I weave my narrative with collective symbolism: dream iconography, Madonna motifs, plant materials, and family photographs. My artistic practice is rooted in rituals that deepen my connections with family, friends, and community. As an archaeologist of memories and dreams, I examine culture and my family’s story through a spiritual lens.

Artist Bio:
H. I. Green (1999) is a multidisciplinary artist from Madison, Mississippi. They obtained a bachelor of arts at Millsaps College in 2021 and have recently completed Mount Royal school of Art Multidisciplinary Program at the 
Maryland Institute College of the Arts (MICA) in Baltimore, MD, earning their MFA.

Having started as a painter, using mostly acrylic paint and oil pastels, Green has 
expanded their practice through a multitude of medioms including printmaking, 
bookmaking, fiber, wood, and sculptural forms. Throughout their time in grad school Green explored themes of familial origins, displaced longing, and systematically aroused confusion, and the antics of being raised in the black religious south.

Social / Website:
insta: h.i.green_

Exhibition Text:
Drawn to the religious and spiritual patterns of the past, H.I. Green uses these motifs to to understand those of the potential patterns of the future as a tool to understand themself and those around them more deeply. In their cyanotype work they recall memories of their own and call on the memories and experiences of their parents, grandparents, and ancestral family. The negative collages for the cyanotype exposures are made using personal imagery from family archives, and then layered with symbolism found in contemporary imagery–both candid and staged–to create exaggerated scenes of traditions and to document the transitions from past to present, looking to the future. Through the use of cyanotype, familial archives, and animated media the artist reflects on the lives, spaces, and places that have surrounded them and others throughout their life in Mississippi. Americana themes perpetuate Green’s work, both in imagery and color choices. This deep connection with Mississippi and its complicated history within our country drives the artist’s exploration of the Black, southern religious aesthetics and rituals that have begged to be expressed through their artistic mind.

Artist Bio:
Joe Smiley (born September 10, 1988 in Mobile, AL)) is an artist based in Jackson, MS,
specializing in contemporary drawing. Working primarily on paper with ink and acrylic
paint markers, Smiley is best known for a distinctive calligraphic visual language
composed of abstract symbols, shapes, and characters reminiscent of ancient writing.
Exploring the magic and mystery of esoteric symbols and texts, Smiley investigates
their ability to convey ideas and emotions through their graphic nature alone. Exhibition Text:
Inspired by the remarkable talent that has influenced Mississippi’s history and culture, artist Kira Cummings highlights the accomplishments and contributions of notable Mississippians in Mississippi Icons. Using pyrography, Cummings carefully details the portraits of nineteen individuals who have either grown up or made an impact on the history of our state. 

“My work explores the intersection of history, fame, and craftsmanship through the medium of woodburning. By creating portraits of famous individuals, I aim to capture not only their likeness but also the deeper essence of their public 
personas—immortalizing their impact in a way that is both tactile and timeless.

Woodburning, or pyrography, allows me to engage with the subject in a deliberate and thoughtful process. The slow, methodical application of heat to wood contrasts with the often fleeting nature of celebrity, grounding these figures in a raw, organic material that evokes permanence. The grain of the wood interacts with each stroke of heat, adding a unique texture that mirrors the complexity of the human experience, suggesting that behind the polished images of fame are nuanced, multifaceted lives.

By rendering these figures in wood, I invite the viewer to reflect on the enduring influence of cultural icons, while also questioning the nature of fame itself. What do we preserve? What is lost? Through these portraits, I aim to offer a moment of stillness, where the viewer can engage not just with the surface of celebrity, but with the lasting impact of those who shape our collective imagination.” - Kira Cummings

Artist Bio:
Kristen Brandt is a self-taught portraitist and embroidery artist living in the Jackson-Metro area. She began her artistic practice with ink-drawn portraits, exploring techniques for achieving value that developed into a more illustrative than photorealistic style. After the passing of her maternal grandmother, Kristen inherited her grandmother’s sewing tools and materials, which prompted her to go entirely in a new direction. While she had learned the basics of embroidery from her paternal grandmother in her youth, she had not applied the skills in many years. Armed with supplies, instruction, and encouragement from these two important women, Kristen began creating hand embroidered patches with designs heavily inspired by animation from films, anime, and video games. Each patch provided an opportunity to learn a new technique or stitch.

She became more confident with a needle in hand and returned to the inked portraits, deciding to re-create them using fabric and thread. The different pieces of fabric are joined together into a single figure and stitched to quilted backgrounds, representing the culmination of a multi-year journey of learning two completely different skills that intertwine seamlessly.

The exhibition’s name, Held Together by Thread, challenges the phrase “holding on by a thread,” indicating that something is precariously positioned due to the frailty of thread as a medium. This exhibition explores the ways in which people are connected to each other through common interests and personal experiences, reinforcing those connections using a medium that shows stitching with even a single strand can forge ironclad bonds. Through engaging with this creative process, she formed a deeper appreciation for each of her grandmothers who led her to this medium and forged meaningful connections with other artists represented in this collection.

 Kristen completed a Masters in Folk Studies at Western Kentucky University in 2016 before starting a job at the Mississippi Arts Commission where she is now the Arts Industry Director. “Held Together by Thread” is the first exhibition of her work.

Born in 1984 in Colombia, Lucia Duque is a Spanish artist currently based in Clinton, Mississippi. 
At the age of four, her family moved to Spain, fleeing the violence that affected Colombia in the 1980s. Her artistic style is a fusion of Latin American and European influences, blending vibrant colors, expressive forms, and deep symbolism.

Migration, identity, and human resilience are central to her work, allowing her to tell both personal and collective stories through art. With decades of experience in painting, teaching, and community engagement, Lucia is passionate about collaborative art. She has led large-scale murals with the NGO Haciendo Barrio in Malasaña, Madrid, encouraging community participation through public art. Additionally, she has taught painting in schools, after-school programs, and workshops for underprivileged children, believing in the power of art as a tool for education and empowerment.Her paintings have been exhibited in Spain and the U.S, including solo exhibitions from her Saastah collection at the Osuna Museum in Seville, the Diputación de Málaga, and Espacio Pozas in Madrid, Exhibition “Making Neighborhood” at Conde Duque Center, Madrid Spain, as well as in California, Indianapolis and Pacesetter Gallery in MS. Her work "Leap of faith" Was exhibited in 2021 at the Art Party in the Mississippi Museum of art. Her most recent mural, located at 201 Clinton Boulevard, MS.
Beyond her personal practice, she has coordinated cultural initiatives such as Welcome Donostia in San Sebastián, Spain, along with various art events and community projects. Exhibition Text:
Pale: Seem less impressive or important. Deficient in color or intensity of color.
 
Ontology: The branch of philosophy that investigates the nature of existence.
 
The work in this series suggests living forms while verging on abstraction. The life depicted is delicate: the forms move, increase in mass, and threaten non-existence relative to the spectator.
 
The systematic and quasi-scientific construction and display methods used in this series are an attempt to recapture the wonder I had as a child visiting natural science museums. The skeletons and fossils on display suggested various aspects and actions of once living things. This prompted me to fill in the blanks of their existence with my limited understanding of the world. The voids and trace elements were active zones filled with muscle, sinew and skin. The poses and traces of movement recorded their intelligence and behavior.
 
I like the idea of memory blending with myth and using research that incorporates speculation. The imaginative reconstruction of beings hopefully can serve as a metaphor for how we generate our own sense of being. 
– Nate Theisen

title: Sitting with Myself in the Dark
creator: Anna Lyons
description: Anna Lyons created this body of work over the past several years as she moved through life in a journey of self discovery and artistic growth. This series of paintings, drawings, ceramics, and found objects represents a curiosity and exploration of identity. The title, Portraits & Other Objects, references both the literal subject of the art in this body of work, as well as Lyons’ fascination with inverting the typical portrait and instead imagining what if objects served as portraits of people, and if people could be represented as objects? Inspired by the legacy of Surrealist painters such as Frida Kahlo, Leonora Carrington, and Hilma af Klint, this series of portraits takes the subject and creates a new world of representation. Each piece begins with nothing more than a thought or even a dream that ignites a creative fire that Lyons harnesses into new work. The resulting dreamlike art opens up an otherworldly environment for the viewer to explore. As you examine the work in this gallery, we invite you to reflect on your own dreams and thoughts and how they could exist in this world.

Artist Bio:
Anna Lyons is an artist raised in southern Louisiana now living in Jackson, MS. She is a BFA graduate of The School of the Art Institute of Chicago with a concentration in Painting, Drawing, and Ceramics. 
 Now walking the path of art education she teaches a diverse range of classes at the Mississippi Museum of Art and is the Director of the after-school art program at The Privette School. Her approach to teaching art starts with introducing her students to fundamental techniques that give them confidence in making art, developing their own style, and then encourage them to break the “rules” they were taught. In the words of one of her long time students “you taught me how to see the world again”. Teaching has become an important part of Anna’s art making process as the different perspectives and conversations remind her how important expressing yourself and how meaningful it is to create something.
 When she is not teaching Anna is working on her current body of work. Using mediums such as oil paint, watercolor, and ceramics she creates worlds inspired by identity, dreams, symbolism, and nature. Fascinated by the imagery in religious and occult art works and the surrealists mission of depicting the unseen within ourselves and in our world Anna’s work incorporates many symbols and motifs we see in these movements. In her work we see the surreal reflection of the artist in the mirror, a portrait surrounded by symbols representing the models interior thoughts, or a depiction of the remembered fragments of a dream. Anna’s work has the intimacy of a diary but with the use of universal symbols the viewer can find themselves within her world.

What happens to the clothing that we stop wearing? Artist Keylon McClendon answers this question with a practice that is deeply rooted in sustainability. Drawing inspiration from the vivid landscapes of the South and the deep cultural narratives of their upbringing, Kimberly’s surrealist paintings are a powerful fusion of dreamlike imagery and raw, introspective symbolism.
 Rooted in an exploration of personal and collective identity, Kimberly’s paintings often feature fluid, distorted forms that challenge conventional understandings of gender and race, inviting the viewer to consider identity as something ever-evolving and multifaceted. The surreal landscapes and figures in their work act as metaphors for the lived experiences of marginalized communities, with a focus on reclaiming and redefining the boundaries of identity.
A product of both deep introspection and the rich traditions of Southern Black culture, Kimberly's art pushes the boundaries of visual storytelling. Through vibrant colors, distorted shapes, and symbolic imagery, they create a dialogue about the complexities of self-discovery, non-conformity, and transformation.
